findings.claim: “For the Edexcel Part (a) extract question (15 marks, AO2)… For Part (b) (25 marks, AO1 + AO3)…”
findings.truth: Edexcel Section A (Shakespeare) is a two-part question worth 20 marks for part (a) (AO2 only, on a printed extract of about 30 lines) and 20 marks for part (b) (AO1 15 + AO3 5). The 15 + 25 split is another board's shape.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1102-1113 (two-part question, part a AO2 on a ~30-line extract, part b AO1 and AO3) and the raw-mark table at lines 1312-1400 (20 / 20 / 40 for Section A).

findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across lessons 1-7 are labelled “15 marks — Extract Response” or “25 marks — Essay Response”, and every mark scheme runs a band ladder scaled to 15 or 25 marks (e.g. “Top band (13-15)”, “Top band (21-25)”).
findings.truth: Both parts of the Edexcel Shakespeare question are worth 20 marks. Every label becomes “20 marks” and every ladder is rescaled to 17-20 / 13-16 / 9-12 / 5-8 / 1-4. The old ladders also used the label “Top band” twice and “Lower band”, which is not the house ladder.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1102-1113 and 1312-1400. Same error family as the sister Edexcel Much Ado unit.

findings.claim: Sebastian is credited with “In nature there’s no blemish but the mind; / None can be called deformed but the unkind” in the body text, in practice question 5, in knowledge check 3 and in flashcard 13.
findings.truth: The couplet is Antonio’s, spoken in 3.4 as he is arrested and believes Sebastian has denied him. Sebastian never says it.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1526 lines 3339-3343: “ANTONIO. But O how vile an idol proves this god! / Thou hast, Sebastian, done good feature shame. / In nature there’s no blemish but the mind…” (line 3342, inside 3.4 = lines 2708-3404).

findings.claim: “When Orsino says Cesario’s lip ‘is more smooth and rubious’ than a woman’s…”
findings.truth: The line is “Diana’s lip / Is not more smooth and rubious” (1.4). Clipping it drops the negative and reverses the comparison; Orsino says a goddess’s lip is no smoother than Cesario’s.

findings.claim: “Olivia acknowledges that Malvolio has been ‘most notoriously abused’, she sends a servant after him to make peace.”
findings.truth: Olivia says “He hath been most notoriously abus’d”. Orsino is the one who calls for the peace: “Pursue him, and entreat him to a peace”. The lesson’s next paragraph already says this correctly, so the two sentences contradict each other.

findings.claim: Sir Toby quoted as “If he may be conveniently delivered, I am now so far in offence with my niece…”
findings.truth: Five words are missing from the middle: “If he may be conveniently delivered, I would he were, for I am now so far in offence with my niece…”

findings.claim: Question 5 sets an extract “to the end of Viola’s aside” and its mark scheme rewards “the aside form (private truth shared with audience but hidden from Olivia)”.
findings.truth: “I am not what I am” is dialogue spoken straight to Olivia, who answers it (“I would you were as I would have you be”). There is no aside anywhere in 3.1. A student rewarded for analysing “the aside form” would be analysing a form that is not there.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1526 lines 2455-2458; no stage direction “Aside” occurs between lines 2193 and 2491 (3.1).

findings.claim: “paradox” is defined as “an expression in which the meaning is the opposite of what the words appear to say, or where contradictory terms are placed together for effect”.
findings.truth: The first half of that defines irony and the second half defines oxymoron. A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself but still points to a truth. The same wrong wording sits in the inline data-def in content_html.
findings.evidence: Standard GCSE literary-terms definition; the lesson’s own practice question 3 correctly calls “witty fool / foolish wit” a chiasmus.

findings.claim: “Understanding these conventions is essential for the Edexcel 1ET0 exam.”
findings.truth: A bare spec code in a lesson field is a banned string for the house validator. “the Edexcel exam” carries the same meaning.

findings.claim: Feste “is also the only character who moves freely between both households”, repeated as a flashcard question.
findings.truth: Viola crosses between Orsino’s court and Olivia’s house repeatedly as Orsino’s messenger, and so do Valentine and Curio. What is true of Feste alone is that he is welcome in both as an entertainer. As written, the flashcard has a second correct answer.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1526: Viola is sent to Olivia in 1.4 and returns in 2.4; Feste sings for Orsino in 2.4 and is paid by him in 5.1.

findings.truth: The Italian is voglio. The lesson body already spells it correctly, so the flashcard contradicts the article.
findings.evidence: content_html of the same lesson: “from the Italian mal + voglio”.

findings.claim: Question 1 sets “Act 1, Scene 1, lines 1–15… to ‘That strain again! it had a dying fall.’”; lesson 2 question 5 sets “lines 19–22… to ‘E’er since pursue me.’”
findings.truth: “That strain again” is line 4 of the speech, not line 15; line 15 is “That it alone is high fantastical.” In lesson 2 the quoted passage runs to about line 24 in standard lineation, not 22. Both mark schemes assume the longer passage.

findings.claim: “His opening line sets the tone: ‘For what says Quinapalus? Better a witty fool than a foolish wit.’”
findings.truth: The quotation and the scene are right (1.5) and Quinapalus is indeed Shakespeare’s invention, but this is not Feste’s opening line. His first line in the play is “Let her hang me: he that is well hanged in this world needs to fear no colours.” Not worth an edit; nothing here costs marks.

findings.claim: The 21 part (a) practice extracts run from a single line (lesson 5 question 5: “I’ll be revenged on the whole pack of you”) to about 25 lines, and several give no boundary at all (“Focus on one specific scene or exchange”).
findings.truth: Edexcel prints an extract of approximately 30 lines for part (a). Students practising on one-line or four-line ‘extracts’ are not rehearsing the real task. Two options: (a) extend each extract to a ~30-line span, which means re-authoring 21 question stems and re-checking each mark scheme against the longer passage; or (b) leave the stems and accept them as focused drills. Recommend (a) but it is a re-authoring job, not a correction, and it would ripple into the mark schemes.

findings.claim: “It is too hard a knot for me to untie” (content, practice question 1, flashcard 4).
findings.truth: The standard text elides to “for me t’untie” to keep the pentameter. The lesson’s expansion changes nothing a marker would penalise, so it is not worth three edits and a re-narration.

findings.claim: Question 1 bounds the extract “to ‘I say this house is dark.’”
findings.truth: The line reads “I am not mad, Sir Topas. I say to you this house is dark.” Two words are dropped. The flashcard in the same lesson quotes it correctly, so a student meets both forms.

summary: The unit is built on another board's question shape: all 42 practice questions and the lesson 1 exam tip claim a 15-mark part (a) and a 25-mark part (b), where Edexcel Section A is 20 + 20. Beyond that the exam framing in lesson 7 is correct (AO2 only on part a, AO1 and AO3 on part b, closed book, ~30-line extract), the quotations are overwhelmingly verbatim, and the only substantive content error is Antonio's 3.4 couplet credited to Sebastian in four places.
